content: Families with preterm or low-birth-weight (LBW) infants may value home visiting services, but it is unclear whether they find these services more or less acceptable compared to other forms of care. For all infants, a minimum of four postnatal care visits is recommended, with additional visits tailored specifically for preterm and LBW infants. The frequency, duration, and intensity of these visits should align with national and local healthcare guidelines and be informed by clinical judgment. Healthcare facilities should follow national or local guidance regarding infrastructure, equipment, and supplies. Health workers at all levels can provide home visits, but standardized training, supervision, and monitoring packages are essential. Further guidance on follow-up care is under development and will be published separately. There is no specific evidence on the feasibility and equity of home visiting interventions for preterm or LBW infants. However, home visiting is a core component of health programs for both term and preterm infants in many countries, regardless of income level. Parental leave policies should address the unique needs of caregivers of preterm or LBW infants, including extended leave and financial support. These policies should consider the costs and burdens faced by families, such as long hospital stays, multiple medical appointments, transportation, and caregiving for other family members. While some countries have parental leave policies for preterm infants, global expansion of such policies is recommended. Families of preterm and LBW infants are at increased risk of financial hardship, stress, anxiety, and depression. Leave from work and financial support are critical to help families care for their infants and manage associated costs, such as transportation, equipment, and hospitalization. Government policies play a vital role in ensuring families receive the necessary financial and workplace support. However, there is limited research on the effectiveness of parental leave policies for families of preterm or LBW infants. Implementation of care recommendations should begin during the antenatal period or at birth and follow national and local healthcare guidelines. Health workers, including social care staff, should provide support and referrals for parental leave and entitlements. Equity in care delivery must be prioritized, and barriers to implementation, such as family or health worker behaviors and healthcare organization challenges, should be addressed. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified significant knowledge gaps requiring primary research. These include understanding the long-term outcomes of preterm and LBW infants, optimizing breastfeeding and donor milk use, evaluating the safety and effectiveness of probiotics and emollients, and improving family involvement in care. Research should also focus on scaling up interventions like kangaroo mother care (KMC) and digital home visits. The dissemination of recommendations will involve WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional associations, and other stakeholders. Recommendations will be made available online and in print, with translations into multiple languages. Technical meetings and evidence briefs will support the adoption and implementation of these guidelines. Monitoring and evaluation of the recommendations will occur at various levels, with indicators such as neonatal mortality, early breastfeeding, postnatal care, and KMC coverage. The guidelines will be updated regularly using a living guidelines approach, with new evidence incorporated as it becomes available.
